`nc`: send and receive over TCP or UDP.

## Synopsis

<strong>nc</strong> \[<strong>-u</strong>\] \[<strong>-b</strong>\] \[<strong>-p</strong> <em>port</em>\] <em>address port</em>\
<strong>nc</strong> \[<strong>-u</strong>\]\
<strong>-l</strong> \[<strong>-p</strong>\] <em>port</em>

## Description

<strong>nc</strong> (netcat) sends what it reads from standard input over the network, through the computer's network cards, and writes what comes back to standard output. <em>address</em> is a network card's address (its id, as <strong>lsdev -i</strong> shows it, with or without its <strong>id:</strong> prefix).

Over TCP (the default) it connects to <em>port</em> at <em>address</em>, or with <strong>-l</strong> listens on <em>port</em> and takes one connection. Then it sends what it reads and writes what comes, until the other side ends; at the end of its input it says it's done sending, so the other side reads its end.

With <strong>-u</strong>, UDP: each read (a line, from a terminal) is a datagram to <em>port</em> at <em>address</em>, or <strong>broadcast</strong> for every card the computer's cards reach (a wired card's cables, a WLAN card's range). What comes back to its port is written out. It ends when standard input ends. With <strong>-l</strong>, it writes each datagram that comes, and sends what it reads to whoever sent the last one, until it's stopped (^C).

## Options

<strong>-u</strong>
: UDP, not TCP.

<strong>-l</strong>
: Listens on <em>port</em>.

<strong>-p</strong> <em>port</em>
: The port it sends from (or listens on, with <strong>-l</strong>). Without it, a free one is given (32768 to 60999).

<strong>-b</strong>
: Taken, and needed for nothing: mcos sends to <strong>broadcast</strong> without SO\_BROADCAST set.

## Exit status

0 when it's done; 1 for a bad option or port, or when it can't connect or send (no network card: "Network is unreachable"; no card took it: "No route to host"; nothing listening: "Connection refused").

## Examples

```text
nc -l 7 > /tmp/heard
nc 1b9c0e-6f0c-4e0f-9a43-7d2f3c1a5e88 7 < notes
nc -ul 7 > /tmp/heard
echo hello | nc -u 1b9c0e6a-6f0c-4e0f-9a43-7d2f3c1a5e88 7
echo all | nc -ub broadcast 7
```

## Notes

mcos has UDP and TCP but no IP: an address is a network card's, and the network is what the cards reach, with nothing routed between networks (a wired card and a WLAN card are two networks). A card never drops a frame: the other card takes it, or the sender hears why not at once ("No buffer space available": it's busy, its queue full or no program taking data there; "No route to host": no card there in reach), and nothing tries again but the software. So a datagram that's sent reached the other card; it's lost there only when no program has its port, or its socket's queue is full, as UDP's are. TCP loses nothing: it tries again what wasn't taken, or wasn't acknowledged. A datagram or a connection to the computer's own card, or a broadcast, reaches its own programs too.

GNU and OpenBSD netcat over UDP stay after standard input ends, until <strong>-q</strong> or <strong>-w</strong> says; this one ends at once, as with <strong>-q 0</strong>. Over TCP it says it's done sending at the end of its input, as OpenBSD's <strong>-N</strong> does.

A network card can turn its computer on while it's off (Wake-on-LAN): a frame for it holding its wake message, anywhere in the data, presses the power button. A program sets the message (an empty one: none) with a socket's ioctl, as Linux's ethtool does:

```text
local sys = require("sys")
sys.ioctl(sys.socket(), "ETHTOOL_SWOL", {name = "wlan0", wake = "letmein"})
```

Then, from another computer: <strong>echo letmein \| nc -ub broadcast 9</strong> (port 9, discard, is the usual one; any will do). Interfaces are named as Linux's: <strong>eth0</strong> for the first wired card, <strong>wlan0</strong> for the first WLAN card.
